page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.2 latency column; §18.3.4 'Scope note'; §18.8 mini-case Tier 1 and the SLO check
quoted_clause: | 70B 4-bit GGUF | $0.15 | 800 | energy only | ... **Tier 1 (4-bit GGUF):** Handles 80% of queries (FAQ, account lookup). Runs on edge nodes (AMD Ryzen 7950X, 64 GB RAM). observed: The latency column is never defined as time-to-first-token or as full generation latency, and under the full-generation reading the printed values are physically impossible by roughly two orders of magnitude. A 70B 4-bit model is ~35 GB of weights; a Ryzen 7950X with dual-channel DDR5-5600 sustains roughly 70-90 GB/s, so each generated token requires streaming ~35 GB, i.e. ~0.4-0.5 s/token. A 250-token request therefore takes ~100-120 s, not 600 ms. The 600 ms and 800 ms figures are only defensible as time-to-first-token, which the chapter never says. The mini-case's central conclusion (Tier 1 violates the 500 ms SLO) is therefore reached with a number that is wrong by ~200x under the natural reading, and the 'recalculate with a feasible Tier 1' step depends on the 250 ms GPU figure being a comparable quantity.
correction: Define the column explicitly (TTFT, or full request latency, or both) and re-derive the values. For the CPU 4-bit tier, either state TTFT (~0.5 s) and label the SLO gate as a TTFT gate, or replace the value with a defensible full-generation latency and let the mini-case's conclusion follow from the corrected number. Apply the same definition to §18.4's 'Latency p95 per model' metric so the metric and the SLO share a unit.
evidence: 35 GB / ~75 GB/s = ~0.47 s per token; 250 tokens = ~117 s. The chapter's own §18.3.4 scope note says these are 'not the canonical TTFT/TPOT SLO (Ch 4)', which leaves the quantity undefined. The mini-case's SLO gate compares a per-request figure against a 500 ms per-request deadline, while §18.4 defines the fleet metric as 'p95 of token-level latency per model'.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.2 cost table 'Basis' column and the 'Basis note (reconciled with Ch16's TCO)' paragraph
quoted_clause: | 70B dense FP16 | $2.50 | 120 | capital + energy | | 70B dense 8-bit | $1.25 | 250 | public cloud [1P] | | 70B MoE 8-bit | $1.00 | 300 | public cloud [1P] | | 70B 4-bit GGUF | $0.15 | 800 | energy only | ... the mixed-fleet *savings* conclusion below depends only on the relative per-model rates, not on the absolute self-host basis.

The claim that the savings conclusion depends only on the relative rates is false when the rates come from different cost bases: a cloud list price for an 8-bit model is not comparable to a self-amortized FP16 rate, and an energy-only rate omits the dominant cost term for a local 70B deployment (the host).

The $23.75/hr single-FP16 baseline is a self-hosted amortized rate; the $8.31/hr 8-bit line is a cloud price. page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Tool-call latency budget' and §4 'Multi-step reasoning cost'; propagates to §8 'Lesson' and 'Architectural actions'
quoted_clause: On 8×H100 the per-turn agent step averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context; tool backends (search, SQL) add 50–150 ms depending on data volume. So per-turn orchestration overhead L_agent ≈ 220 ms (median).

The chapter calls L_agent 'the per-turn cost of the loop *around* the model' and then includes 'the LLM's short decision step to formulate the tool call', which is model inference, not overhead around it.
correction: Either (a) redefine L_agent as the tool-only leg (≈100–133 ms/turn) and rename β accordingly, or (b) state explicitly that the 120 ms decision step assumes prefix reuse of the grown prefix (≈865 new tokens ≈ 100 ms prefill) and that under the no-reuse policy the per-turn model work is ≈2.9 s. A 120 ms 'agent step' is reachable only if the decision step's prefill is reduced to the ~865 newly appended tokens (≈100 ms), i.e. under prefix reuse — an assumption the L_agent paragraph never states, and one that contradicts the no-reuse framing in which β is presented. quoted_clause: "a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s, with a 200-rps burst buffer (an arrival-rate buffer: outage bursts queue for drain rather than being served live - 200 rps x ~7 TFLOP ~= 1.4 PFLOPS exceeds one H100's ~0.989 PFLOPS peak)"

The chapter nevertheless closes with 'The customer's vague excitement became a defensible, bounded, shippable scope', presenting a single-GPU recommendation whose own arithmetic contradicts the SLO it claims to meet.
correction: State the burst duration and rate; compute the queue depth (arrival rate x duration) and the drain time at the sustainable rate; then state explicitly that burst-window requests miss the 3 s SLO and choose one of: (a) a separate burst SLO or degraded mode, (b) size for the burst (>= 4 H100s for prefill alone), or (c) a named fallback path. evidence: 200 rps x (2 x 7e9 params x 500 tokens) = 200 x 7e12 FLOP/s = 1.4e15 FLOP/s = 1.4 PFLOPS vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak (the chapter's own figures). At the 30-40% sustained MFU used elsewhere in the book, one H100 delivers ~0.30-0.40 PFLOPS, so the burst alone needs ~3.5-4.7 GPUs. No burst duration is stated anywhere in the mini-case.

quoted_clause: §3.1: "the number of distinct prompt-pattern classes an adversary can successfully submit through all user-facing entry points" | §4.1: "**PIES** | DERIVED | Unique, non-redundant prompt-injection patterns across all entry points" | §8: "PIES has dropped from 217 to 143 after adding a prompt-scanning guardrail"
observed: The chapter carries two incompatible definitions of its central metric. §3.1 defines PIES as the classes an adversary can *successfully* submit (a success-conditioned count); §4.1 defines it as *unique patterns* (a pattern-space count). The worked arithmetic in §3.1 implements only the pattern-space reading — 4 x 8 x 6 x 4 = 768 candidates, deduplicated to 217, with no success criterion applied anywhere. The mini-case then reports a PIES *drop* (217 -> 143 -> 138) caused by adding a guardrail, which is only meaningful under the success reading; under the §4.1 pattern-space reading a guardrail cannot change the pattern space at all, so the headline trajectory of the chapter's capstone is unexplained by the metric as defined in the metric table.
correction: Choose one definition and make every occurrence match. Recommended: keep the §3.1 arithmetic but rename it (e.g. 'candidate pattern space CPS = 217'), and define PIES as the subset of candidate classes that produced at least one guardrail bypass in the cycle; then the mini-case's 217 -> 143 -> 138 becomes 'successful classes', and Table 24-1's PIES row must be re-derived under that definition. Alternative: keep PIES as the pattern-space count, hold it constant across cycles, and move the guardrail effect entirely onto the red-team win rate and guardrail-trigger rate rows (which already carry it), rewriting §6 consequence 1 and §8 accordingly. Update §4.1's definition and the §5 mistake row to match whichever is chosen.
evidence: §3.1 arithmetic: 4 entry points x 8 delimiters x 6 templates x 4 context segments = 768; 'After deduplication by normalized edit distance at a fixed threshold ... the unique exposure surface is PIES = 217' — no success filter. §4.1 metric row omits 'successfully'. §6 consequence 1: 'reducing PIES by roughly a third - ~34% (the §8 mini-case's worked instance: 217 -> 143)' — a guardrail changing a pattern count. §5 mistake table: 'Deduplicate by normalized syntax and report PIES' — again the pattern-space reading.

page_hint: Ch. 7 §6 Architecture Consequence, KV quantization bullet
quoted_clause: This is a *memory* lever, orthogonal to bandwidth/compute fixes — the architect pulls it when the KV floor, not decode bandwidth, binds.
observed: KV quantization is described as orthogonal to bandwidth, but reducing KV precision also reduces the bytes of K/V state read during decode, which can directly relieve KV-bandwidth pressure. It is not compute-reducing, but it is not bandwidth-orthogonal.
correction: Rewrite as: 'KV quantization is primarily a capacity lever; it can also reduce KV read bandwidth during decode, but it does not reduce attention FLOPs. Pull it when KV capacity binds, and benchmark it when decode bandwidth may also be limiting.'
evidence: Decode reads historical K/V tensors from HBM each token. Halving KV bytes per element reduces KV read traffic, subject to layout, metadata, and kernel behavior. The same section elsewhere correctly says FP8 KV halves raw tensor bytes; that byte reduction is exactly what can affect bandwidth-bound decode.

page_hint: Ch 9 §6 (Architecture Consequence), anchors also in §3 Option A and §6 cost paragraph
quoted_clause: keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case (§9.3)

correction: Rewrite §6 to separate the two layers. State that an eight-node data-parallel job uses NVLink/NVSwitch for intra-node exchanges and InfiniBand/RoCE for inter-node exchanges; compare InfiniBand versus Ethernet only for the inter-node portion, and compare NVLink only for the intra-node portion. If the chapter wants to retain the 11×/180× numbers, label them explicitly as comparisons between an eight-rank single-host collective and an eight-rank cross-host collective, not as fabric choices for the same job. Remove or qualify the capex/opex paragraph so it does not imply that NVSwitch-inside-node and 200GbE RoCE are mutually exclusive cluster designs.
evidence: The §9.3 example explicitly says the NVLink case is 'not a memory-feasible eight-replica training deployment' and is a communication-only comparison. A data-parallel job across eight nodes with eight GPUs per node spans 64 ranks, not eight ranks inside one host. NVLink inside a node and InfiniBand/RoCE between nodes are complementary layers, not mutually exclusive alternatives. The 11×/180× ratios therefore compare different group sizes and topology scopes, not two fabrics serving the same collective.
